specPoints.text: understand the biological consequences of pollution of water by sewage
understand the biological consequences of eutrophication caused by leached minerals from fertiliser

primer.text: Water pollution reaches rivers as leached fertiliser and as sewage, and both end the same way, with oxygen stripped from the water. This note follows eutrophication step by step and shows how sewage multiplies bacteria, kills sensitive species and lowers biodiversity.

lessons.title: Eutrophication Step by Step
lessons.opening: Fertiliser washed off fields carries nitrates into lakes and streams, and those minerals trigger eutrophication: surface plants and algae explode in growth, then die, and the decomposers that break them down strip the water of oxygen.
keyPoints: Minerals from fertilisers are leached into water bodies, causing eutrophication.
Fertilisers are rich in nitrates, so aquatic plants and algae overgrow at the water surface.
Shaded plants below the surface die and are broken down by decomposers.
The growing decomposer population respires, using up oxygen until many aquatic organisms die.

low.restatement: Extra nitrates grow a carpet of plants, the carpet dies, and the clean-up crew uses up all the oxygen.
low.analogy: A feast that fills the hall with guests, then leaves so much washing-up that the water supply runs dry.
low.examPointer: Learn the sequence — leaching, overgrowth, shade deaths, decomposer boom, oxygen crash.

medium.restatement: The cascade runs on cause and effect: nitrate-rich leaching fuels surface growth, the surface layer shades out the plants beneath, decomposition of the dead matter swells the bacterial population, and bacterial respiration drives dissolved oxygen down until fish and other aquatic organisms cannot survive.
medium.analogy: A canopy of billboards blots out the shops below, the bankrupt shops pile up, and the rubbish crews burn through the town's oxygen handling the pile.
medium.examPointer: Explain the oxygen loss through decomposer respiration — that chain of reasoning earns the marks.

check.stem: Which minerals leaching from fields drive eutrophication?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Limestone calcium is not the fertiliser driver here.
Eroded iron is unrelated to fertiliser leaching.
Road salt is a different pollutant entirely.

check.stem: What happens first after nitrates enter a lake?

options.text: Aquatic plants and algae overgrow at the water surface
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Fish deaths come last, after oxygen collapses.
Temperature is not the first event.
Decomposers boom after the plant die-off.

check.stem: Why do plants below the surface die during eutrophication?

options.text: The surface overgrowth cuts the light reaching them
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They run out of carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is not the limiting factor being blocked.
Nitrates feed plants; shade is what kills them.
Fish grazing is not the mechanism.

check.stem: How do decomposers lower dissolved oxygen?

options.text: Their respiration consumes the oxygen dissolved in the water
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Respiration uses oxygen; it does not emit a poison.
Gill clogging is not the documented route.
Water volume is unchanged; oxygen is consumed.

check.stem: What is the final stage of eutrophication?

options.text: Oxygen falls so low that many aquatic organisms die
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The lake becomes saltier than the sea
options.explanation: Salinity is not the endpoint described.
The boom collapses once light and oxygen fail.
No rock forms; the sequence ends in oxygen depletion.

check.stem: State what leaching means in the context of fertilisers.
check.modelAnswer: Leaching is the washing of soluble minerals, such as nitrates from fertiliser, out of soil into nearby water bodies.

check.stem: Name the process that follows fertiliser leaching into lakes.
check.modelAnswer: Eutrophication is the process that follows when fertiliser minerals are leached into lakes and streams.

check.stem: Explain why decomposer numbers rise during eutrophication.
check.modelAnswer: Decomposer numbers rise because the shaded aquatic plants die and leave abundant dead material for bacteria and fungi to feed on.

check.stem: A farmer sprays fertiliser before heavy rain. Predict the lake downstream.
check.modelAnswer: Rain leaches the nitrates into the lake, triggering algal overgrowth, plant death, a decomposer boom and falling oxygen, so fish and other aquatic organisms die.

lessons.title: Sewage in the Water
lessons.opening: Sewage entering waterways feeds aerobic bacteria that multiply on the waste, and their respiration drains the dissolved oxygen that sensitive aquatic species need, collapsing biodiversity and raising the risk from pathogenic bacteria.
keyPoints: Sewage enters waterways when sewers overflow or farm waste washes off fields in heavy rain.
Aerobic bacteria feeding on the sewage increase in number.
The bacteria reduce dissolved oxygen, so oxygen-sensitive aquatic organisms die.
Only low-oxygen survivors remain, so biodiversity decreases, and pathogenic bacteria also increase.

low.restatement: Sewage feeds bacteria, the bacteria breathe up the oxygen, and only the hardy survivors remain.
low.analogy: A crowd of guests at a party consuming every breath of air in the room until only the least demanding stay.
low.examPointer: Pair the two consequences: biodiversity falls, and pathogenic bacteria rise.

medium.restatement: The mechanism mirrors eutrophication without the plant stage: sewage supplies biological waste for aerobic bacteria, bacterial respiration depletes dissolved oxygen, oxygen-sensitive species die leaving a low-diversity community, and the polluted water also harbours more pathogenic bacteria.
medium.analogy: A landfill dumped into a river: the clean-up crews multiply, exhaust the oxygen, and the only residents left are the ones that like mess and disease.
medium.examPointer: State the route into waterways — overflowing sewers or washed-off farm waste — when asked how pollution happens.

check.stem: How does sewage commonly reach rivers?

options.text: When sewers overflow or heavy rain washes agricultural waste off fields
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Pipes carry treated water to taps, not sewage to rivers.
Evaporation does not transport sewage.
Roots cannot carry sewage into rivers.

check.stem: Which organisms multiply first when sewage enters a stream?

options.text: Aerobic bacteria that feed on the biological waste
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Algae bloom on nitrates in eutrophication, not on sewage waste directly.
Fish larvae decline in polluted water.
Denitrifiers act on nitrates in soil, not sewage waste.

check.stem: What happens to dissolved oxygen after a sewage spill?

options.text: It falls because the growing bacteria respire heavily
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It rises with the extra waste
options.explanation: Waste feeds bacteria whose respiration consumes oxygen.
Bacterial respiration changes it measurably.
No such conversion happens.

check.stem: Which aquatic organisms survive a severe sewage pollution event?

options.text: Only species that tolerate low oxygen concentrations
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Oxygen-sensitive species die first.
Size does not grant oxygen tolerance.
Producers are not the survivors highlighted here.

check.stem: Why does sewage pollution raise a second, invisible danger?

options.text: Because pathogenic bacteria increase alongside the pollution
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Radioactivity plays no part here.
Fish do not turn venomous from sewage.
Oxygen never becomes toxic; pathogens are the hidden hazard.

check.stem: State the effect of sewage on aerobic bacteria in waterways.
check.modelAnswer: Sewage provides biological waste, so aerobic bacteria feeding on it increase in number.

check.stem: State the effect of sewage pollution on the biodiversity of an aquatic ecosystem.
check.modelAnswer: Biodiversity decreases because oxygen-sensitive organisms die and only low-oxygen survivors remain.

check.stem: Explain why sewage and fertiliser leaching produce similar oxygen crashes.
check.modelAnswer: Both events feed large microbial populations whose respiration consumes dissolved oxygen, so both drive oxygen down until sensitive aquatic organisms die.

check.stem: A town reports both an overflow and a fish kill downstream. Order the events.
check.modelAnswer: The overflow released sewage, aerobic bacteria multiplied on the waste, respiration cut dissolved oxygen, and the fish died from oxygen shortage.

glossary.definition: The process in which leached fertiliser minerals trigger plant overgrowth, decay and oxygen loss in water.
The washing of soluble minerals from soil into nearby water bodies by rain.
Bacteria that need oxygen to respire, which multiply on sewage waste in water.
Bacteria that cause disease, which increase in water polluted by sewage.
